choices.label: A
choices.rationale: Doubles the molar mass to 36.0 g mol⁻¹ (double-counting the two hydrogens) before dividing, giving 9.00/36.0 = 0.250 mol.

choices.label: B
choices.rationale: Correct: n = m/M = 9.00 g ÷ 18.0 g mol⁻¹ = 0.500 mol. The grams cancel to leave moles, and the answer carries three significant figures to match the data.

choices.rationale: Inverts the ratio and divides molar mass by mass (18.0/9.00), giving 2.00 instead of moles.

choices.label: D
choices.rationale: Multiplies mass by molar mass instead of dividing (9.00 × 18.0), giving 162.

A. C–H
B. O–F
C. Cs–F
D. N–O

Choices:
A. C–H
B. O–F
C. Cs–F
D. N–O

choices.label: A
choices.rationale: Incorrect. The electronegativity difference between C (2.55) and H (2.20) is only about 0.35, which is characteristic of a nonpolar (or only very slightly polar) covalent bond, not an ionic one.

choices.label: B
choices.rationale: Incorrect. The electronegativity difference between O (3.44) and F (3.98) is about 0.54, placing this bond firmly in the polar covalent category — small compared to the difference for a metal–nonmetal pair like Cs–F.

choices.label: C
choices.rationale: Correct. Cs (0.79) and F (3.98) have an electronegativity difference of about 3.19, the largest of the choices. This large difference reflects the ease with which the large electronegativity difference favors substantial electron transfer from Cs to F and predominantly ionic bonding, producing a bond with predominantly ionic character (as in the compound CsF).

choices.label: D
choices.rationale: Incorrect. The electronegativity difference between N (3.04) and O (3.44) is only about 0.40, indicating a polar covalent bond between two nonmetals, not an ionic interaction.

body:
Which of the following species requires an expanded (greater than octet) valence shell around its central atom in its best Lewis structure?

A. CO2
B. ClF3
C. SiCl4
D. PF3

Choices:
A. CO2
B. ClF3
C. SiCl4
D. PF3

choices.label: A
choices.rationale: Incorrect. In CO2, carbon forms two double bonds to oxygen, giving carbon exactly 8 electrons (4 bonding pairs' worth of shared electrons) — a complete octet with no expansion needed.

choices.label: B
choices.rationale: Correct. The conventional Lewis structure of ClF3 has three Cl-F bonds and two lone pairs on chlorine, placing five electron domains and ten electrons around the central period-3 atom. The trigonal-bipyramidal electron-domain arrangement gives a T-shaped molecule.

choices.label: C
choices.rationale: Incorrect. Silicon forms 4 single bonds to Cl, using exactly 8 electrons around Si (a standard tetrahedral octet structure), even though Si is a period-3 element capable of expansion in other compounds.

choices.label: D
choices.rationale: Incorrect. Phosphorus forms 3 single bonds to F and retains 1 lone pair, giving exactly 8 electrons (a complete octet) around P — no expansion occurs here, unlike in PF5.

body:
The nitrite ion, NO2-, is represented by two equivalent resonance contributors in which nitrogen forms one N=O double bond and one N–O single bond (with the negative charge delocalized by resonance). In this Lewis structure, what is the formal charge on the singly-bonded oxygen atom?

A. 0
B. −1
C. −2
D. +1

Choices:
A. 0
B. −1
C. −2
D. +1

choices.label: A
choices.rationale: Incorrect. A formal charge of 0 applies to the doubly-bonded oxygen in this structure (FC = 6 − (4 lone-pair electrons + 2 bonding electrons) = 0), not the singly-bonded oxygen, which has three lone pairs rather than two.

choices.label: B
choices.rationale: Correct. The singly-bonded O has 3 lone pairs (6 nonbonding electrons) and 1 bond (contributing 1 electron in the formal charge count). Formal charge = (6 valence electrons) − (6 nonbonding electrons + 1) = 6 − 7 = −1. This is consistent with the overall −1 charge on NO2- once the neutral doubly-bonded O and neutral N are accounted for.

choices.label: C
choices.rationale: Incorrect. Assigning four lone pairs to the singly bonded oxygen would give a formal charge of -3, not -2; the actual singly bonded oxygen has formal charge -1.

choices.label: D
choices.rationale: Incorrect. This would result from using an incorrect number of valence electrons for oxygen (e.g., treating it as having 8 valence electrons instead of 6) or miscounting the bonding contribution.

What are the electron-domain geometry and molecular (molecular-domain) shape of SF4?

A. Trigonal bipyramidal electron-domain geometry; seesaw molecular shape
B. Trigonal bipyramidal electron-domain geometry; trigonal pyramidal molecular shape
C. Octahedral electron-domain geometry; square pyramidal molecular shape
D. Tetrahedral electron-domain geometry; seesaw molecular shape

Choices:
A. Trigonal bipyramidal electron-domain geometry; seesaw molecular shape
B. Trigonal bipyramidal electron-domain geometry; trigonal pyramidal molecular shape
C. Octahedral electron-domain geometry; square pyramidal molecular shape
D. Tetrahedral electron-domain geometry; seesaw molecular shape

choices.text: Trigonal bipyramidal electron-domain geometry; seesaw molecular shape
choices.label: A
choices.rationale: Correct. Sulfur (6 valence electrons) forms 4 bonds to F atoms and retains 1 lone pair, giving 5 total electron domains. Five domains arrange as a trigonal bipyramid; the lone pair preferentially occupies an equatorial position to minimize 90° repulsions, leaving the 4 bonded F atoms in a seesaw (seesaw) molecular shape.

choices.text: Trigonal bipyramidal electron-domain geometry; trigonal pyramidal molecular shape
choices.label: B
choices.rationale: Incorrect. Trigonal pyramidal shape results from a tetrahedral (4-domain) electron geometry with one lone pair, as in NH3 — not from a 5-domain trigonal bipyramidal arrangement with one lone pair, which instead gives a seesaw shape.

choices.text: Octahedral electron-domain geometry; square pyramidal molecular shape
choices.label: C
choices.rationale: Incorrect. This describes a central atom with 6 electron domains (5 bonds + 1 lone pair, as in ClF5), but S in SF4 has only 5 total electron domains (4 bonding + 1 lone pair), not 6.

choices.text: Tetrahedral electron-domain geometry; seesaw molecular shape
choices.label: D
choices.rationale: Incorrect. A tetrahedral electron-domain geometry arises from only 4 electron domains, which would not accommodate 4 bonding pairs plus a lone pair (5 domains total). The seesaw molecular shape is correctly identified, but it necessarily arises from a trigonal bipyramidal (5-domain) electron geometry, not a tetrahedral one.

Which substance is expected to have the highest normal boiling point?

A. CH4
B. CH3Cl
C. CH3OH
D. C2H6

Choices:
A. CH4
B. CH3Cl
C. CH3OH
D. C2H6

choices.label: A
choices.rationale: Incorrect. CH4 is a small nonpolar molecule whose molecules attract one another only through relatively weak London dispersion forces.

choices.label: B
choices.rationale: Incorrect. CH3Cl is polar and has dipole-dipole attractions, but it cannot form hydrogen bonds with itself because its hydrogen atoms are bonded to carbon.

choices.label: C
choices.rationale: Correct. CH3OH molecules form hydrogen bonds through the O-H group. For these particular substances, that strong intermolecular attraction produces the highest normal boiling point.

choices.label: D
choices.rationale: Incorrect. C2H6 is nonpolar. Although it is more polarizable than CH4, its molecules experience only London dispersion forces and its boiling point is below that of CH3OH.

CH3F and CH3OH have similar molar masses (34 g/mol and 32 g/mol, respectively), yet CH3OH has a substantially higher boiling point (65C) than CH3F (-78C). What best explains this difference?

A. CH3OH molecules are larger, so they experience much stronger London dispersion forces than CH3F.
B. Intermolecular attractions are limited to dipole-dipole interactions and London dispersion forces because the molecule has no H bonded to N, O, or F.
C. CH3F is ionic while CH3OH is molecular, so CH3F should have the lower boiling point regardless of intermolecular forces.
D. Fluorine's higher electronegativity compared to oxygen means CH3F molecules attract each other more strongly, so CH3F should have the higher boiling point.

Choices:
A. CH3OH molecules are larger, so they experience much stronger London dispersion forces than CH3F.
B. Intermolecular attractions are limited to dipole-dipole interactions and London dispersion forces because the molecule has no H bonded to N, O, or F.
C. CH3F is ionic while CH3OH is molecular, so CH3F should have the lower boiling point regardless of intermolecular forces.
D. Fluorine's higher electronegativity compared to oxygen means CH3F molecules attract each other more strongly, so CH3F should have the higher boiling point.

choices.text: CH3OH molecules are larger, so they experience much stronger London dispersion forces than CH3F.
choices.label: A
choices.rationale: Incorrect: the two molecules have nearly identical size and molar mass, so their dispersion forces are comparable. Dispersion force strength depends primarily on molecular size/polarizability, not on this difference.

choices.text: Intermolecular attractions are limited to dipole-dipole interactions and London dispersion forces because the molecule has no H bonded to N, O, or F.
choices.label: B
choices.rationale: Correct: CH3OH has an O-H bond, so its molecules form strong hydrogen bonds with one another. CH3F is polar but has no H bonded directly to N, O, or F, so it is limited to dipole-dipole attraction together with the London dispersion forces every molecule has. Hydrogen bonding accounts for the much higher boiling point of CH3OH.

choices.text: CH3F is ionic while CH3OH is molecular, so CH3F should have the lower boiling point regardless of intermolecular forces.
choices.label: C
choices.rationale: Incorrect: both CH3F and CH3OH are covalent molecular substances, not ionic compounds. Ionic character is not the relevant distinction here.

choices.text: Fluorine's higher electronegativity compared to oxygen means CH3F molecules attract each other more strongly, so CH3F should have the higher boiling point.
choices.label: D
choices.rationale: Incorrect: this both misreads the data (CH3F has the lower boiling point) and misapplies electronegativity, bond polarity alone doesn't determine whether hydrogen bonding is possible; that requires an H atom bonded directly to N, O, or F, which CH3F lacks.

A solid sample conducts electricity well in both its solid and molten states, is malleable (can be hammered into sheets without shattering), and has a moderately high melting point. What type of solid is this sample most likely to be?

A. An ionic solid, such as an alkali halide
B. A metallic solid, such as a transition metal
C. A covalent network solid, such as silicon dioxide
D. A molecular solid, such as solid iodine

Choices:
A. An ionic solid, such as an alkali halide
B. A metallic solid, such as a transition metal
C. A covalent network solid, such as silicon dioxide
D. A molecular solid, such as solid iodine

choices.text: An ionic solid, such as an alkali halide
choices.label: A
choices.rationale: Incorrect: ionic solids conduct electricity only when molten or dissolved in water, because the ions must be mobile to carry charge; in the rigid solid lattice the ions cannot move, so the solid state does not conduct. Ionic solids are also brittle, not malleable.

choices.text: A metallic solid, such as a transition metal
choices.label: B
choices.rationale: Correct: metallic solids consist of a lattice of cations surrounded by a sea of delocalized valence electrons. These mobile electrons conduct electricity in both the solid and molten states, and the nondirectional metallic bonding allows layers of cations to slide past each other under stress, producing malleability rather than fracture.

choices.text: A covalent network solid, such as silicon dioxide
choices.label: C
choices.rationale: Incorrect: covalent network solids have all atoms held in a rigid lattice of directional covalent bonds, with no mobile charge carriers, so they do not conduct electricity as solids or (in most cases) as liquids. They are also extremely hard and brittle, not malleable, and typically have very high (not moderate) melting points.

choices.text: A molecular solid, such as solid iodine
choices.label: D
choices.rationale: Incorrect: molecular solids are held together by weak intermolecular forces between discrete molecules, giving them low melting points and no electrical conductivity in either the solid or liquid state, since there are no ions or delocalized electrons to carry charge.

A rigid 2.00 L container holds 0.500 mol of an ideal gas at 27C. What is the pressure of the gas? (R = 0.08206 L*atm/(mol*K))

A. 0.554 atm
B. 6.15 atm
C. 12.3 atm
D. 24.6 atm

Choices:
A. 0.554 atm
B. 6.15 atm
C. 12.3 atm
D. 24.6 atm

choices.label: A
choices.rationale: Incorrect: this results from plugging in T = 27 (treating the given Celsius value as if it were already in kelvin) instead of converting to 300 K first. The ideal gas law requires temperature in kelvin.

choices.label: B
choices.rationale: Correct: convert 27C to 300 K, then solve P = nRT/V = (0.500 mol)(0.08206 L*atm/mol*K)(300 K) / 2.00 L = 12.309 / 2.00 = 6.15 atm.

choices.label: C
choices.rationale: Incorrect: this is nRT/V computed with n = 1 mol instead of the given 0.500 mol, i.e., the moles term was dropped from the calculation.

choices.label: D
choices.rationale: Incorrect: this comes from multiplying by volume instead of dividing by it (P = nRT*V rather than P = nRT/V), inverting the relationship between pressure and volume in the ideal gas law.

Separate rigid containers hold samples of He(g) and O2(g) at the same temperature. According to kinetic molecular theory, which statement correctly compares the two samples?

A. The average kinetic energy is the same in both samples, and the average molecular speed is also the same, since both are at the same temperature.
B. The average kinetic energy is the same in both samples, but He atoms have a greater average speed than O2 molecules.
C. O2 molecules have greater average kinetic energy than He atoms because O2 has greater mass, and O2 also has greater average speed.
D. He atoms have greater average kinetic energy than O2 molecules because He moves faster, and O2 has greater average speed.

Choices:
A. The average kinetic energy is the same in both samples, and the average molecular speed is also the same, since both are at the same temperature.
B. The average kinetic energy is the same in both samples, but He atoms have a greater average speed than O2 molecules.
C. O2 molecules have greater average kinetic energy than He atoms because O2 has greater mass, and O2 also has greater average speed.
D. He atoms have greater average kinetic energy than O2 molecules because He moves faster, and O2 has greater average speed.

choices.text: The average kinetic energy is the same in both samples, and the average molecular speed is also the same, since both are at the same temperature.
choices.label: A
choices.rationale: Incorrect: average kinetic energy depends only on temperature and is indeed equal, but average speed also depends on molar mass (KE = half m v squared), so equal kinetic energy with unequal mass means unequal average speeds.

choices.text: The average kinetic energy is the same in both samples, but He atoms have a greater average speed than O2 molecules.
choices.label: B
choices.rationale: Correct: kinetic molecular theory states that average kinetic energy depends only on absolute temperature, so it is equal for He and O2 at the same T. Since KE is the same for both but He has a much smaller molar mass, He atoms must move faster on average to have the same average kinetic energy as the heavier O2 molecules.

choices.text: O2 molecules have greater average kinetic energy than He atoms because O2 has greater mass, and O2 also has greater average speed.
choices.label: C
choices.rationale: Incorrect: average kinetic energy depends only on temperature, not molar mass, so it cannot be greater for the heavier gas at equal temperature. In fact, the heavier O2 molecules have the lower average speed, not the higher one.

choices.text: He atoms have greater average kinetic energy than O2 molecules because He moves faster, and O2 has greater average speed.
choices.label: D
choices.rationale: Incorrect: this statement is internally contradictory (claiming O2 has greater speed while also saying He moves faster) and incorrectly ties average kinetic energy to speed differences rather than to temperature, which is the actual determinant of average kinetic energy.

body:
Under which set of conditions would a real gas be expected to deviate most significantly from ideal gas behavior, and why?

A. High temperature and low pressure, because molecules move so quickly that intermolecular attractions and molecular volume become significant.
B. Low temperature and high pressure, because molecules are forced close together (making their finite volume non-negligible) and move slowly enough for intermolecular attractive forces to noticeably affect their motion.
C. High temperature and high pressure, because both factors independently increase the frequency of molecular collisions with the container walls.
D. Low temperature and low pressure, because the gas volume becomes negligible under these conditions.

Choices:
A. High temperature and low pressure, because molecules move so quickly that intermolecular attractions and molecular volume become significant.
B. Low temperature and high pressure, because molecules are forced close together (making their finite volume non-negligible) and move slowly enough for intermolecular attractive forces to noticeably affect their motion.
C. High temperature and high pressure, because both factors independently increase the frequency of molecular collisions with the container walls.
D. Low temperature and low pressure, because the gas volume becomes negligible under these conditions.

choices.text: High temperature and low pressure, because molecules move so quickly that intermolecular attractions and molecular volume become significant.
choices.label: A
choices.rationale: Incorrect: high temperature and low pressure is actually the regime where real gases behave most ideally. Fast-moving molecules spend less time near each other (minimizing the effect of attractive forces) and low pressure means large intermolecular spacing, so molecular volume is negligible compared to container volume.

choices.text: Low temperature and high pressure, because molecules are forced close together (making their finite volume non-negligible) and move slowly enough for intermolecular attractive forces to noticeably affect their motion.
choices.label: B
choices.rationale: Correct: at low temperature, molecules move slowly enough for intermolecular attractive forces to noticeably affect their motion, and at high pressure, molecules are forced close together, making their finite molecular volume non-negligible relative to the container volume. Together these two effects produce the greatest deviation from ideal-gas behavior.

choices.text: High temperature and high pressure, because both factors independently increase the frequency of molecular collisions with the container walls.
choices.label: C
choices.rationale: Incorrect: increased collision frequency with the walls is not what causes deviation from ideality; deviations arise from non-negligible molecular volume and intermolecular attractions, and high temperature actually counteracts these effects by keeping molecules moving fast and spending less time interacting.

choices.text: Low temperature and low pressure, because the gas volume becomes negligible under these conditions.
choices.label: D
choices.rationale: Incorrect: at low pressure the gas occupies a large volume with widely spaced molecules, so molecular volume is negligible and this actually favors ideal behavior; it is the combination of low temperature with high (not low) pressure that produces the greatest deviation.

body:
As the temperature of water increases, the solubility of a gas such as O2(g) in the water generally decreases. Which statement best explains this observation?

A. At higher temperatures, gas molecules have greater average kinetic energy, allowing more of them to overcome the weak intermolecular attractions holding them in solution and escape into the gas phase.
B. At higher temperatures, hydrogen bonds between water molecules strengthen, trapping more gas molecules within the solvent structure.
C. Temperature breaks O2 molecules apart into atoms, so fewer O2 molecules remain dissolved.
D. The decrease is caused only by evaporation of water, which makes the remaining dissolved oxygen concentration appear lower.

Choices:
A. At higher temperatures, gas molecules have greater average kinetic energy, allowing more of them to overcome the weak intermolecular attractions holding them in solution and escape into the gas phase.
B. At higher temperatures, hydrogen bonds between water molecules strengthen, trapping more gas molecules within the solvent structure.
C. Temperature breaks O2 molecules apart into atoms, so fewer O2 molecules remain dissolved.
D. The decrease is caused only by evaporation of water, which makes the remaining dissolved oxygen concentration appear lower.

choices.text: At higher temperatures, gas molecules have greater average kinetic energy, allowing more of them to overcome the weak intermolecular attractions holding them in solution and escape into the gas phase.
choices.label: A
choices.rationale: Correct. Gas dissolution is generally exothermic; heating favors the gas phase and decreases dissolved O2 at constant O2 partial pressure.

choices.text: At higher temperatures, hydrogen bonds between water molecules strengthen, trapping more gas molecules within the solvent structure.
choices.label: B
choices.rationale: Incorrect. Increasing temperature weakens, not strengthens, intermolecular attractions such as hydrogen bonding; this reasoning also does not explain reduced gas solubility.

choices.text: Temperature breaks O2 molecules apart into atoms, so fewer O2 molecules remain dissolved.
choices.label: C
choices.rationale: Incorrect. The decrease in dissolved O2 is not due to dissociation into atoms under these conditions.

choices.text: The decrease is caused only by evaporation of water, which makes the remaining dissolved oxygen concentration appear lower.
choices.label: D
choices.rationale: Incorrect. The main effect is the temperature-dependent gas-solution equilibrium, not simply water evaporation.

A colored solution has a molar absorptivity of 1.50 x 10^3 M^-1 cm^-1 at its wavelength of maximum absorbance. When placed in a cuvette with a 1.00 cm path length, the solution's absorbance is measured as 0.750. What is the molar concentration of the solution?

A. 1.13 x 10^3 M
B. 5.00 x 10^-4 M
C. 2.00 x 10^3 M
D. 7.50 x 10^-1 M

Choices:
A. 1.13 x 10^3 M
B. 5.00 x 10^-4 M
C. 2.00 x 10^3 M
D. 7.50 x 10^-1 M

choices.label: A
choices.rationale: Incorrect. This results from multiplying A by epsilon (0.750 x 1500) instead of dividing, misapplying the Beer-Lambert law A = epsilon*b*c.

choices.label: B
choices.rationale: Correct. Rearranging A = epsilon*b*c gives c = A/(epsilon*b) = 0.750/(1.50 x 10^3 x 1.00) = 5.00 x 10^-4 M.

choices.label: C
choices.rationale: Incorrect. This comes from computing epsilon*b/A instead of A/(epsilon*b), inverting the correct rearrangement of the Beer-Lambert equation.

choices.label: D
choices.rationale: Incorrect. This treats the absorbance value itself as the concentration, ignoring both epsilon and b entirely.

A chemist needs to recover acetone (boiling point 56 °C) from a homogeneous mixture of acetone and water (boiling point 100 °C). The two liquids are miscible and do not form an azeotrope. Which technique is most appropriate, and why?

A. Filtration, because it separates the two liquids based on differences in particle size.
B. Distillation, because heating the mixture selectively vaporizes the lower-boiling acetone, which can then be condensed and collected separately from the higher-boiling water.
C. Paper chromatography, because it separates substances based on their particle size as they pass through the paper.
D. Recrystallization, because cooling the mixture causes the higher-boiling liquid to solidify out of solution.

Choices:

B. Distillation, because heating the mixture selectively vaporizes the lower-boiling acetone, which can then be condensed and collected separately from the higher-boiling water.

choices.label: B
choices.rationale: Correct. Acetone and water differ in boiling point by about 44 °C and do not form an azeotrope, so heating selectively vaporizes the lower-boiling acetone; the vapor is condensed and collected, leaving the higher-boiling water behind.

choices.label: C

choices.label: D

A student reacts 5.4 g of Al (molar mass 27.0 g/mol) with 3.2 g of O2 (molar mass 32.0 g/mol) according to the balanced equation 4Al(s) + 3O2(g) -> 2Al2O3(s) (molar mass Al2O3 = 102.0 g/mol). What mass of Al2O3 is produced, assuming the reaction goes to completion?

A. 6.8 g
B. 10.2 g
C. 8.6 g
D. 15.3 g

Choices:
A. 6.8 g
B. 10.2 g
C. 8.6 g
D. 15.3 g

choices.label: A
choices.rationale: Correct. mol Al = 5.4/27.0 = 0.200 mol; mol O2 = 3.2/32.0 = 0.100 mol. Complete consumption of 0.200 mol Al would require 0.150 mol O2, but only 0.100 mol O2 is available, so O2 is the limiting reactant. mol Al2O3 = 0.100 mol O2 x (2 mol Al2O3/3 mol O2) = 0.0667 mol x 102.0 g/mol = 6.8 g.

choices.label: B
choices.rationale: Incorrect. This treats Al as the limiting reactant, but there is not enough O2 present to consume all the Al, so Al is not actually the limiting reactant.

choices.label: C
choices.rationale: Incorrect. This simply adds the given masses of the two reactants (5.4 g + 3.2 g) rather than using the balanced equation and molar masses to find the mass of product formed.

choices.label: D
choices.rationale: Incorrect. This correctly identifies O2 as limiting but inverts the mole ratio, using 3 mol Al2O3 per 2 mol O2 instead of the correct 2 mol Al2O3 per 3 mol O2.

Aqueous solutions of Pb(NO3)2 and KI are mixed, forming a yellow precipitate: Pb(NO3)2(aq) + 2KI(aq) -> PbI2(s) + 2KNO3(aq). Which equation correctly represents the net ionic equation for this reaction?

A. Pb2+(aq) + 2I-(aq) -> PbI2(s)
B. Pb(NO3)2(aq) + 2KI(aq) -> PbI2(s) + 2KNO3(aq)
C. Pb2+(aq) + 2NO3-(aq) + 2K+(aq) + 2I-(aq) -> PbI2(s) + 2K+(aq) + 2NO3-(aq)
D. K+(aq) + NO3-(aq) -> KNO3(s)

Choices:
A. Pb2+(aq) + 2I-(aq) -> PbI2(s)
B. Pb(NO3)2(aq) + 2KI(aq) -> PbI2(s) + 2KNO3(aq)
C. Pb2+(aq) + 2NO3-(aq) + 2K+(aq) + 2I-(aq) -> PbI2(s) + 2K+(aq) + 2NO3-(aq)
D. K+(aq) + NO3-(aq) -> KNO3(s)

choices.label: A
choices.rationale: Correct. K+ and NO3- appear unchanged on both sides of the complete ionic equation, so they are spectator ions and are removed, leaving only the ions that form the precipitate.

choices.label: B
choices.rationale: Incorrect. This is the molecular (formula unit) equation, not the net ionic equation, it has not been separated into ions or had spectator ions removed.

choices.label: C
choices.rationale: Incorrect. This is the complete ionic equation; it still includes the spectator ions K+ and NO3-, which must be cancelled from both sides to obtain the net ionic equation.

choices.label: D
choices.rationale: Incorrect. This misidentifies the spectator ions as the species that react. KNO3 is soluble and remains dissociated in solution, so K+ and NO3- do not combine to form a solid.

A. Decomposition reaction, because a single compound breaks down into two or more simpler substances.

choices.text: Decomposition reaction, because a single compound breaks down into two or more simpler substances.

choices.text: Combination (synthesis) reaction, because two products form from the reactants.
choices.label: B

choices.text: Single-replacement reaction, because calcium changes bonding partners.

choices.text: Combustion, because CO2 is produced during heating.
choices.label: D
choices.rationale: Incorrect. Producing CO2 does not by itself make a reaction combustion; combustion requires reaction with O2 as a reactant.

Dinitrogen pentoxide decomposes according to the equation 2 N2O5(g) -> 4 NO2(g) + O2(g). At a certain point during the reaction, O2 is forming at a rate of 0.015 M/s. What is the rate of disappearance of N2O5 at that same instant?

A. rate = k[X][Y]
B. rate = k[X]^2[Y]
